title: The Work, Torah Teaching and Legacy of Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa: A Comprehensive Study of His Life, His Writings, His Thought and His Martyr's Death in Toledo

The Work, Torah Teaching and Legacy of Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa: A Comprehensive Study of His Life, His Writings, His Thought and His Martyr's Death in Toledo
Historical Context and Chapters of His Life: From Wandering to the Sanctification of God's Name in Toledo
The socio-religious and cultural environment in Christian Spain in the 14th century was marked by growing political and religious tension, which reached its tragic peak in the pogroms of 5151 (1391) [cite: 1, 2]. Out of this dark reality, full of upheavals, arose the figure of Rabbi Yisrael ben Yosef Alnakawa (who appears in the sources also as Alnakaua or Ankawa), one of the great sages of Spain, a liturgical poet, preacher, kabbalist and halakhic decisor, who belonged to the circle of disciples of the study hall of the Rosh (Rabbenu Asher ben Yechiel) in Toledo [cite: 1, 2, 3].
Over the childhood and youth of Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa there hangs a historical obscurity, but from the autobiographical details embedded in the introduction to his central work there emerges a life course saturated with hardships, uprooting and forced mobility [cite: 3]. Alnakawa describes his experiences as those of one who moved and wandered across the lands of Spain before finding relative rest: "Most of my days I was moving about and wavering like a solitary bird... for the hand of time has driven me away, and the hurling of a mighty man has hurled me... and I was not at ease, nor was I quiet, nor did I rest" [cite: 3]. The sense of impermanence and suffering that accompanied the physical and social dispersal fed his spiritual world, and became a powerful creative engine that drove him to gather the Torah sources and to formulate an organizing moral conception [cite: 3].
Upon his arrival in Toledo (Tulitula) – which was at that time the senior spiritual and Talmudic centre of Castilian Jewry – Alnakawa joined the circles of students of the yeshiva of the Rosh and his disciples [cite: 2, 3]. This centre of study brought together the French-Ashkenazi tradition of learning, which was marked by sharp textual analysis and dynamic Talmudic discussion, and the local Spanish tradition, which excelled in systematic order, philosophical thought and a tendency towards halakhic and homiletic codification [cite: 1, 2]. The influence of the Rosh on Alnakawa is evident in his immense command of the sources of the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmud, alongside a conscious combination of aggadic midrashim and practical conduct [cite: 1].
The end of the story of Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa's life is interwoven with the national tragedy that befell the communities of Spain. On the 17th of Tammuz, 5151 (1391), with the outbreak of the wave of riots and cruel decrees spread by the incited Christian mob, Alnakawa was arrested in Toledo and was required to convert to Christianity [cite: 1, 2]. Facing the threat of death, he chose to sanctify the Name publicly and not to deny his faith [cite: 1]. According to the historical traditions, Alnakawa was put to death, ascending the pyre while holding a Torah scroll in his hand, together with the son of the Rosh [cite: 2, 3, 4]. Because of his tragic and public death in defence of the faith, the title "the Holy" clung to him in the literature of the generations [cite: 2, 3].
Out of this destruction there grew a branching spiritual and familial continuity in North Africa. Rabbi Yisrael's son, Rabbi Ephraim Alnakawa, fled the decrees of 5151 from Spain to North Africa and settled in the city of Tlemcen in Algeria [cite: 2, 3, 5, 6]. There he became a spiritual leader of decisive influence, a judge, a philosopher (the author of the work "Shaar Kevod HaShem" – "The Gate of the Glory of the Lord") and a physician, whose name is linked with popular traditions of miraculous deeds and whose grave became a place of pilgrimage [cite: 2, 5, 6]. This dynasty continued to produce prominent sages, halakhic decisors and liturgical poets in the Jewry of the Maghreb throughout the generations [cite: 3, 7].
His Magnum Opus: "Menorat ha-Maor" – Structure, Methodology and Contents
The central and most prominent work of Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa is the book "Menorat ha-Maor" ("The Lamp of Illumination"), known in research and in Torah literature as "Menorat ha-Maor ha-Kadmon" ("the Ancient Menorat ha-Maor") [cite: 3]. The work was written in pure, original and fluent Hebrew, and constitutes a broad Torah-ethical encyclopedia [cite: 1, 3]. The book merges concrete halakhic rulings, aggadic homilies of the Sages, ethical ideas and kabbalistic practices [cite: 1]. The work opens with a complex liturgical poem containing an acrostic in which the author signed his name: "I, Israel, the author, son of Rabbi Yosef, may his rest be in Eden, son of Alnakaua", followed by a prose introduction that sets out his conceptual approach and the structure of the book [cite: 1, 2].
The book is divided into 23 comprehensive chapters. The first 20 chapters are devoted to a survey of the 613 commandments and the foundational issues of Jewish life, with each chapter centring on one main subject and gathering the halakhot, midrashim and sayings of the Sages relevant to it [cite: 1]. The last three chapters are built in a unique lexicographic-thematic format that collects aggadic sayings according to opening words or overarching themes [cite: 1].
The table below details the content structure of the 23 chapters of the work "Menorat ha-Maor" by Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa:
Chapter number | Chapter name / main topic | Main contents and focal points of the halakhic and ethical discussion
Chapter 1 | The Chapter on Charity | The virtue of giving charity, giving in secret, the laws of redeeming captives, concern for the poor and social kindness [cite: 1, 8].
Chapter 2 | The Chapter on Prayer | The complexity of the order of prayer, communal prayer, the prayer leader, the recitation of the Shema, the Amidah, blessings and festivals [cite: 1].
Chapter 3 | The Chapter on Repentance | The power and virtue of repentance, the stages of atonement, accepting suffering with love, and ethical instruction for the righteous and for sinners [cite: 1].
Chapter 4 | The Chapter on Humility | Ways of attaining humility, distancing oneself from pride, arrogance and humbleness of spirit as an existential value [cite: 1].
Chapter 5 | The Chapter on Torah Study | The duty of Torah study, Torah for its own sake, combining Torah with a trade and derekh eretz, and the punishment for neglect of Torah study [cite: 1].
Chapter 6 | The Chapter on the Commandments | Studying in order to practise, the laws of circumcision, redemption of the firstborn son, mezuzah, challah, mourning and the laws of consolation [cite: 1].
Chapter 7 | The Chapter on Acts of Loving-Kindness | The importance of kindness, visiting the sick, accompanying the dead, eulogy, and acts of loving-kindness through body and money [cite: 1].
Chapter 8 | Honouring Sabbaths and Festivals | Observance of the Sabbath, Sabbath delight, the covenant of the Sabbath, the sanctity of the festivals and appointed times [cite: 1].
Chapter 9 | The Chapter on Honouring Father and Mother | The greatness of the commandment of honouring one's begetters, the details of the practical duties, reverence for father and mother and the limits of obedience [cite: 1].
Chapter 10 | The Chapter on Marrying a Wife | The pairing of man, the virtues of the modest woman, the sanctity of the home, distancing oneself from fornication, and marital fidelity [cite: 1].
Chapter 11 | The Chapter on Raising Children | The moral instruction of children, the father's duty to teach his son Torah, the community ordinance on hiring teachers of young children [cite: 1].
Chapter 12 | The Chapter on Business Dealings | Honesty in commerce, distancing oneself from robbery and fraud, the laws of lending to the poor and keeping away from forbidden profits [cite: 1].
Chapter 13 | The Chapter on Judgment and the Judge | The importance of justice and righteousness, the qualities of the proper judge, distancing oneself from bribery and equality before the law [cite: 1].
Chapter 14 | To Rejoice in One's Portion | The virtue of contentment with little, the trait of trust in God, distancing oneself from envy and the pursuit of money [cite: 1].
Chapter 15 | The Chapter on Anger and Wrath | The ugliness of anger, the departure of wisdom at the time of anger, and the virtue of slowness to anger and patience [cite: 1].
Chapter 16 | The Chapter on Flattery and Scoffing | The harm that flattery does to society, the groups of flatterers, and the gravity of the seat of scoffers and of scoffing [cite: 1].
Chapter 17 | The Chapter on Love of Friends | The importance of cleaving to good friends, distancing oneself from dispute and hatred, and love of righteous converts [cite: 1].
Chapter 18 | The Chapter on Evil Speech | The gravity of the prohibition of evil speech and tale-bearing, the punishment of one who speaks ill, and the virtue of silence [cite: 1].
Chapter 19 | Concealing a Fellow's Secret | Keeping secrets, personal loyalty, caution regarding oaths and distancing oneself from falsehood and quarrel [cite: 1].
Chapter 20 | The Chapter on Derekh Eretz | The conduct of Torah scholars, social etiquette, the conduct of women and of the elderly, and rules of human behaviour [cite: 1].
Chapter 21 | Eternal Light | A collection of sayings and aggadot of the Sages that all open with the word "always" (le-olam) [cite: 1].
Chapter 22 | The Chapter "Great" | A collection of sayings and aggadot of the Sages that all open with the word "great" (gadol) [cite: 1].
Chapter 23 | Great Is Peace | A sublime section devoted entirely to the value of peace, its importance in society and between man and God [cite: 1].
This methodological structure testifies to a well-formed pedagogical conception on the part of the author, who avoided creating an abstract halakhic code or, on the other hand, offering moral preaching detached from halakha. The close combination of practical law with its homiletic and conceptual source created a comprehensive guide to Jewish life, intended to shape both the visible deed and the inner world of the learner [cite: 1].
His Torah Teaching, Ethical Reflections and Early Kabbalah
The Torah teaching of Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa expresses a unique synthesis of normative halakha, ethical thought and early Kabbalah [cite: 1, 2]. While many sages of his time tended to create a separation between purely halakhic works and works of ethics or Kabbalah, Alnakawa saw the world of Torah as an organic whole in which the revealed and the hidden, law and character trait, complement one another fully.
One of the most significant aspects of Alnakawa's teaching concerns his attitude to the literature of the esoteric and in particular to the Book of the Zohar [cite: 2]. Alnakawa was among the first of the sages of Spain who cited the Book of the Zohar extensively and integrated its ideas into an ethical-halakhic work intended for the general public [cite: 2]. In his book he designates the Book of the Zohar by the name "Midrash Vayehi Or" [cite: 2]. A phenomenon of the first textual and scholarly importance is that Alnakawa translated the Aramaic passages of the Zohar into pure Hebrew, in order to make them accessible to a reader who did not command the Aramaic language [cite: 2]. Scholars of Kabbalah and of textual transmission have pointed out that the versions of the Zohar embedded in his "Menorat ha-Maor" constitute a rare and early textual testimony to the versions of the Zohar that were in circulation in Spain at the end of the 14th century, a period in which complete manuscripts of the Zohar were extremely rare [cite: 2].
From the moral and intellectual standpoint, Alnakawa placed the rectification of character traits and social sensitivity at the centre of his book. His in-depth discussions in the chapters on charity, business dealings, acts of loving-kindness and the concealment of a secret demonstrate that, in his view, religious holiness is measured not only by asceticism or by the fine points of the commandments between man and God, but first of all by the relations between a person and his fellow, by commercial honesty and by human loyalty [cite: 1]. In the chapter "Torah Study" he stressed the duty to combine study with manual work and derekh eretz, taking a resolute stand against phenomena of exploiting learning for personal gain or for class arrogance [cite: 1].
The concluding section of the book, the chapter "Great Is Peace," offers a glimpse into the spiritual world of an author who lived in a period full of internal disputes and external persecutions [cite: 1]. The placing of the value of peace as the seal of his entire work teaches of a view according to which peace is the vessel that holds all the blessings, and is the ultimate purpose of all 613 commandments and ethical teachings [cite: 1].
The Scholarly and Literary Polemic: The Relation of "Menorat ha-Maor" to Alnakawa and to Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab
Around the work of Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa there developed one of the most fascinating and prolonged polemics in the history of the bibliography and study of Torah literature: the question of the relationship and chronological precedence between the book "Menorat ha-Maor" by Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa and the well-known book "Menorat ha-Maor" composed by Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab [cite: 2, 9, 10, 11].
The book of Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab enjoyed an enormous circulation throughout the generations, was printed in dozens of editions, was translated into Yiddish, Ladino and German, and became a foundational book studied regularly in the communities of Israel [cite: 11, 12]. By contrast, the book of Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa remained in manuscript for hundreds of years and was not widely printed until the 20th century [cite: 2, 3, 9]. With the discovery of Alnakawa's unique manuscript in the Bodleian Library in Oxford and its publication by the scholar Hillel Gershom Enelow in four volumes between the years 1929–1932, a scholarly storm arose [cite: 9, 10, 13, 14, 15]. Enelow argued resolutely that Alnakawa was the original author of the "Menorat ha-Maor ha-Kadmon," and that Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab lived about fifty years after Alnakawa and copied, abridged and adapted Alnakawa's work into his own book [cite: 2, 3, 9, 10]. This claim was accepted for decades among many scholars and bibliographers, and was reflected even in the titling of new editions of the book under the name "Menorat ha-Maor ha-Kadmon" [cite: 3].
However, in the second half of the 20th century Professor Israel Ta-Shma challenged this thesis from its foundations [cite: 2, 10, 11, 16]. By means of meticulous historical and philological analysis, and on the basis of the discovery of an early commentary on Aboab's book that was written as early as the middle of the 14th century, Ta-Shma proved that Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab the First lived and was active in the first half of the 14th century, and therefore his work preceded in time the work of Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa [cite: 11]. Ta-Shma showed that it was Alnakawa who knew Aboab's book, or that the two draw on shared homiletic sources that were widespread in Spain at that time [cite: 2, 10, 11, 16].
Despite the scholarly dispute over chronological precedence, all researchers agree that there is a deep literary and substantive relation between the two works [cite: 2, 10, 11]. However, the features of formulation and structure are completely different. Whereas the work of Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab is based on a division into seven lamps (seven central gates), focuses on moral preaching and a popular homiletic adaptation intended to draw the heart while omitting intricate halakhic discussions [cite: 11, 12, 17], the work of Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa is based on 23 chapters, includes within it a detailed halakhic system, decides practical rulings, incorporates kabbalistic citations translated from the Zohar, and presents a far more encyclopedic and comprehensive character [cite: 1, 2].
Circulation, Legacy and Influence on the Ethical Literature of Later Generations
Although Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa's original work remained hidden away in manuscripts and was not disseminated in print until the 20th century, his teaching had an immense and concealed influence on Jewish ethical and halakhic literature throughout the generations, chiefly through intermediary channels and secondary adaptations [cite: 2, 3, 18].
The main channel through which Alnakawa's teachings seeped into all the Jewish diasporas was the "Sefer ha-Musar" ("The Book of Moral Instruction") composed by Rabbi Yehuda Kalatz (the First), one of the sages of Spain who moved to Tlemcen in Algeria in the second half of the 15th century [cite: 2, 18]. Rabbi Yehuda Kalatz was exposed to the manuscript of Alnakawa's "Menorat ha-Maor," and decided to prepare from it a concise abridgement [cite: 2, 18]. Kalatz omitted the long halakhic pilpul, focused on the ethical instructions and the conduct of character traits, and turned the work into a practical and accessible guide [cite: 2]. This book was first printed in Constantinople in the year 5297 (1537), and afterwards in further editions in Mantua (1561) and in Kraków (1598) [cite: 2, 18]. In preparation for the printing, another sage, Rabbi Moshe Kalatz (one of the kabbalists of Safed), added to it glosses and explanations according to Kabbalah and the Book of the Zohar, which gave the book enormous popularity [cite: 2, 18, 19]. Through Kalatz's "Sefer ha-Musar," Alnakawa's ideas reached the spiritual centre in Safed in the 16th century and the communities of Eastern Europe [cite: 2, 18]. Subsequently, this abridgement served as the basis for the well-known Yiddish ethical book "Lev Tov" ("A Good Heart") by Rabbi Yitzchak ben Eliakum of Posen, which became one of the most widespread books among Ashkenazi Jewry [cite: 2].
In parallel, leading halakhic decisors and kabbalists in the 16th and 17th centuries cited directly and indirectly from Alnakawa's work. Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas, one of the foremost kabbalists of Safed and author of the book "Reshit Chokhmah" ("The Beginning of Wisdom"), inserted into his book entire chapters from Alnakawa's "Menorat ha-Maor," such as the chapter on humility and the chapter on repentance, and relied on them in building his kabbalistic ethical doctrine [cite: 3]. Likewise, Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema), one of the great decisors of Ashkenaz, brought Alnakawa's words and his book many times in his glosses and works [cite: 2]. In his wake, Rabbi Isaiah HaLevi Horowitz (the Holy Shelah) cited Alnakawa's "Menorat ha-Maor" dozens of times in his book "Shenei Luchot HaBerit" ("The Two Tablets of the Covenant"), and adopted his conception which combines law, ethics and the esoteric [cite: 2].
In modern times Alnakawa's work enjoyed a renewed revival [cite: 3, 9]. After the printing of the exemplary scholarly-critical edition in four volumes by Hillel Gershom Enelow in New York (1929–1932) [cite: 9, 15], there appeared in recent years annotated and vocalized Torah editions, such as the "Menorat ha-Maor ha-Kadmon" edited by Rabbi Yosef Alnakawa (a descendant of the author), which returned the book to the table of the study hall in practice [cite: 3].
Conclusions
Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa represents an exemplary figure of a Torah scholar and halakhic decisor who combines profound Talmudic study, exceptional moral sensitivity, and conceptual daring in joining the revealed to the hidden [cite: 1, 2]. His many wanderings and the personal and national tragedy in which he ended his life, in the sanctification of God's Name in Toledo in 1391, turn his work "Menorat ha-Maor" not only into a mighty literary-halakhic creation, but also into a spiritual testament of a generation that was required to stand in the breach against harsh historical upheavals [cite: 1, 3].
His Torah teaching, expressed in the planned division of the 23 chapters of "Menorat ha-Maor," set an encyclopedic model of a Torah of life [cite: 1]. The translation of the Zohar's passages into Hebrew and their early integration in his work attest to his role as a pioneer in making the esoteric teaching accessible to the general public [cite: 2]. Although his work suffered the vicissitudes of history and remained in manuscripts, its conceptual power survived and seeped into the core of Jewish ethical and halakhic literature through the adaptations of Rabbi Yehuda Kalatz, of the author of "Reshit Chokhmah," of the Rema and of the Shelah [cite: 2, 3, 18]. Modern research and the renewed publication of his work have restored to Rabbi Yisrael Alnakawa his proper place on the eastern wall of the sages of Spain and of Jewish thought.
